precepts.text: It grieved them exceedingly that there was come a man to seek the welfare of the children of Israel. They do not like it when we speak up for our people.
precepts.point: The squeaky wheel gets the oil. We will complain, judge, bring out the records, and beg the Lord until he kills our enemies and sets us up, like the widow before the unjust judge. Our enemies want us silent, locked away with our mouths zipped, calling us troublemakers; yes, we are causing trouble, because you are not supposed to be over us. Nehemiah 2:10 shows they grieve when a man comes to seek the welfare of the children of Israel.

note.label: The Image of Dysfunction or the Image of God Which One Are You?

precepts.why:
The Lord has set watchmen upon the walls of Jerusalem “which shall never hold their peace day nor night”. Watchmen pay attention to the condition of the people and to the enemy coming to destroy the people. “ye that make mention of the Lord, keep not silence, And give him no rest, till he establish, and till he make Jerusalem a praise in the earth.”

Nehemiah shows how the enemy takes it when Israel speaks up: “When Sanballat the Horonite, and Tobiah the servant, the Ammonite, heard of it, it grieved them exceedingly that there was come a man to seek the welfare of the children of Israel.” They do not like it when we speak up for our people.

That is why our enemies want us silent, locked away with the key thrown away and our mouths zipped. They call us troublemakers. Yes, we are causing trouble, because you are not supposed to be over us. They want a quiet slave.

The squeaky wheel gets the oil. Quiet people are ignored, and noisy people force others to take action. So we will complain, judge, bring out the records and tell it like it is, and we will beg the Lord and give him no rest, like the widow before the unjust judge, until he kills our enemies and sets Jerusalem up on high.

precepts.text: The Most High says he will cause the enemy to entreat his remnant well in the time of evil; it is not that the heathen love Israel, but that the Lord moves a king or a friend to deal well with them.
precepts.point: The king grants him all this according to the good hand of his God upon him. Nehemiah had already prayed, and the Most High heard him and put it upon the king's heart to allow him to go.

note.label: Nehemiah 2: The King Sends Nehemiah to Rebuild

precepts.why:
Nehemiah asked the king for letters to the governors beyond the river and a letter to Asaph the keeper of the king's forest for timber, “And the king granted me, according to the good hand of my God upon me.” The Most High had said this would happen: “Verily it shall be well with thy remnant; verily I will cause the enemy to entreat thee well in the time of evil and in the time of affliction.”

It is not that the heathen love Israel. It is that the Lord causes the enemy to entreat his remnant well in the time of evil and affliction. Nehemiah had already prayed, and the Most High heard him and put it upon the king's heart to allow him to go. The king's favour was the good hand of God, not the king's own goodwill.

precepts.text: Ezra blessed the Most High for putting it into the heart of the king, showing the good the heathen ruler does is the Lord moving him, not his own love for Israel.
precepts.point: The king grants him all this according to the good hand of his God upon him. Nehemiah had already prayed, and the Most High heard him and put it upon the king's heart to allow him to go.

note.label: Nehemiah 2: The King Sends Nehemiah to Rebuild

precepts.why:
Ezra saw the same thing in his day and knew where it came from: “Blessed be the only Lord God of my fathers, who hath put these things into the heart of the king, to glorify his house that is in Jerusalem”.

Ezra did not bless the king; he blessed the Most High for putting these things into the heart of the king. The good the heathen ruler does is the Lord moving him, not his own love for Israel. So when the king granted Nehemiah his letters and his timber, it was “according to the good hand of my God upon me”, the same hand that moved the king in Ezra's day.

precepts.text: The people of the land weakened the hands of Judah, troubled them in building, and hired counsellors against them to frustrate their purpose, the same hindering spirit against the rebuilding.
precepts.point: When Sanballat the Horonite and Tobiah the servant, the Ammonite, hear of it, it grieves them exceedingly that a man has come to seek the welfare of the children of Israel, the same opposition seen when the nation tried to rebuild before.

note.label: Nehemiah 2: The King Sends Nehemiah to Rebuild

precepts.why:
When Sanballat the Horonite and Tobiah the servant, the Ammonite, heard that a man had come to seek the welfare of the children of Israel, it grieved them exceedingly. This is the same opposition seen when the nation tried to rebuild before: “Then the people of the land weakened the hands of the people of Judah, and troubled them in building, And hired counsellors against them, to frustrate their purpose, all the days of Cyrus king of Persia, even until the reign of Darius king of Persia.”

The people of the land weakened Judah's hands, troubled them in building, and hired counsellors against them to frustrate their purpose, and kept it up from Cyrus to Darius. That same hindering spirit against the rebuilding met Nehemiah the moment he arrived with the king's letters and his escort of captains and horsemen.

precepts.text: The enemies wrote to the king that if the rebellious city were built and the walls set up, the Jews would no more pay toll, tribute, and custom, and so damage the revenue of kings, the same mindset that fears Israel's rebuilding.
precepts.point: When Sanballat the Horonite and Tobiah the servant, the Ammonite, hear of it, it grieves them exceedingly that a man has come to seek the welfare of the children of Israel, the same opposition seen when the nation tried to rebuild before.

note.label: Nehemiah 2: The King Sends Nehemiah to Rebuild

precepts.why:
The enemies in Ezra's day wrote to the king: “Be it known unto the king, that the Jews which came up from thee to us are come unto Jerusalem, building the rebellious and the bad city, and have set up the walls thereof, and joined the foundations. Be it known now unto the king, that, if this city be builded, and the walls set up again, then will they not pay toll, tribute, and custom, and so thou shalt endamage the revenue of the kings.”

They called Jerusalem the rebellious and the bad city, and their argument was money: if the walls go up, the Jews will no more pay toll, tribute and custom, and the revenue of kings will suffer. That is the same mindset that fears Israel's rebuilding. Sanballat and Tobiah were grieved exceedingly for the same reason: a man had come to seek the welfare of the children of Israel, and Israel restored is a loss to those who profit from Israel down.

points: Nehemiah, two and ten. That is the one. Remember these verses, brothers.

When Sanballat the Horonite, and Tobiah the servant, the Ammonite, heard of it, it grieved them. It grieved our enemies. So our people feel the grief that the enemies will levy upon us, because someone is actually coming to give us a proper image of ourselves.
When they heard that someone came to seek the welfare of the people. The people in Mississippi, they felt that repression, even that psychological repression, even though we were not even there yet.

It grieved them exceedingly. Exceedingly. They got very angry. That there was come a man to seek the welfare of the children of Israel. When we came to Mississippi, we seek the welfare of the brothers and sisters that are living with boarded-up spirits, and they were afraid because of the spirit that was on our enemies.

That is how our enemies feel when we go into these areas and lift our brothers and sisters up. They start saying that we are a bunch of haters, and we are spreading lies, and they try to say all of those things — but meanwhile the people live with dilapidated spirits. They live with boarded-up spirits. So when we come to seek their welfare, our enemies get exceedingly mad, exceedingly vexed and grieved, because we sought our brothers. We sought our sisters.

So when we go to these areas, we are seeking the welfare of the people. And our enemies do not want that. That is the reason why they try to ban us on YouTube. They try to ban us with the different platforms, and lie on us and say that we are about hating and this and that and the other.

points: In the month Nisan in the twentieth year of Artaxerxes the king, wine is before him and Nehemiah takes up the wine and gives it to the king. This is Artaxerxes the first, the king that came after Ahasuerus of the book of Esther.

note.label: Nehemiah 2: The King Sends Nehemiah to Rebuild

points: Nehemiah had not before been sad in the king's presence, for a cupbearer must be of a cheerful countenance, so the king asks why his countenance is sad seeing he is not sick, saying this is nothing but sorrow of heart, and Nehemiah is very sore afraid.

note.label: Nehemiah 2: The King Sends Nehemiah to Rebuild

points: Nehemiah answers, Let the king live for ever, why should not his countenance be sad when the city, the place of his fathers' sepulchres, lies waste and its gates are consumed with fire.

note.label: Nehemiah 2: The King Sends Nehemiah to Rebuild

points: The king asks what request he makes, and Nehemiah prays to the God of heaven before he answers, seeking the Most High even in that moment before the king.

note.label: Nehemiah 2: The King Sends Nehemiah to Rebuild

points: Nehemiah asks that if it please the king and if his servant have found favour, the king would send him to Judah, to the city of his fathers' sepulchres, that he may build it.

note.label: Nehemiah 2: The King Sends Nehemiah to Rebuild

points: The king, the queen also sitting by him, asks how long his journey would be and when he would return, so Nehemiah sets him a time, and it pleased the king to send him.

note.label: Nehemiah 2: The King Sends Nehemiah to Rebuild

points: Nehemiah asks for letters to the governors beyond the river to convey him until he comes into Judah, and a letter to Asaph the keeper of the king's forest to give him timber for the beams of the gates, the wall, and the house he would enter.
The king grants him all this according to the good hand of his God upon him. Nehemiah had already prayed, and the Most High heard him and put it upon the king's heart to allow him to go.

note.label: Nehemiah 2: The King Sends Nehemiah to Rebuild

points: Nehemiah comes to the governors beyond the river and gives them the king's letters, and the king had sent captains of the army and horsemen with him, an armed escort to see him safe.

note.label: Nehemiah 2: The King Sends Nehemiah to Rebuild

points: When Sanballat the Horonite and Tobiah the servant, the Ammonite, hear of it, it grieves them exceedingly that a man has come to seek the welfare of the children of Israel, the same opposition seen when the nation tried to rebuild before.

note.label: Nehemiah 2: The King Sends Nehemiah to Rebuild

points: Nehemiah comes to Jerusalem and is there three days, then arises in the night with a few men, telling no man what his God had put in his heart to do, for saying too much could ruin the plan.

note.label: Nehemiah 2: The King Sends Nehemiah to Rebuild

points: He goes out by night through the gate of the valley, past the dragon well to the dung port, and views the walls of Jerusalem broken down and the gates consumed with fire, then goes on to the gate of the fountain and the king's pool.

note.label: Nehemiah 2: The King Sends Nehemiah to Rebuild

points: The rulers do not know where he went or what he did, neither had he yet told the Jews, priests, nobles, rulers, or the rest that did the work.

note.label: Nehemiah 2: The King Sends Nehemiah to Rebuild

points: Nehemiah then tells them, Ye see the distress that we are in, how Jerusalem lies waste and its gates are burned; come and let us build up the wall of Jerusalem that we be no more a reproach.

note.label: Nehemiah 2: The King Sends Nehemiah to Rebuild

points: He tells them of the good hand of his God upon him and the king's words, and they say, Let us rise up and build, and strengthen their hands for this good work.

What is admirable in Nehemiah, as in Ezra, is that he never says the work was of his own knowledge or wisdom, but that the Lord's hand was upon him, and he puts that same vision on the men around him so they strengthen their hands to help.

note.label: Nehemiah 2: The King Sends Nehemiah to Rebuild

points: When Sanballat the Horonite, Tobiah the Ammonite, and Geshem the Arabian hear it, they laugh them to scorn, despise them, and ask what this thing is, and whether they will rebel against the king.

note.label: Nehemiah 2: The King Sends Nehemiah to Rebuild

points: Nehemiah answers that the God of heaven will prosper them, and his servants will arise and build, but the mockers have no portion nor right nor memorial in Jerusalem. There was no shame in what he came to do.
